**Status:** draft 0.1 (Phase 0). Sections marked **Decision** record a convention that both implementations must follow. All decisions D1–D6 were settled on 2 November 2026; new decisions are added as *open* and must be settled before the corresponding code is written. # Purpose and scope

This document defines the econometric conventions shared by the R package `unitroottools` and the Python package UnitRoot-Tools. It is language-neutral: it states *what* is computed and *how results are reported*, not how either language implements it.

Rules:

1. The specification is updated **before** the code.
2. Each implementation may cover a different subset of the specification, but anything it implements must conform to it.
3. Conformance is checked through shared numerical fixtures (@sec-validation).
4. A backend (e.g. urca) may compute a result only if the result can be reported in the form required by @sec-contract. Every result records which engine computed it.

# Data and deterministic specifications

## Input series

- The input is a real, finite, one-dimensional, equally spaced series $y_1,\dots,y_T$. R accepts `numeric`, `ts`, `zoo` and `xts`, and also tidy objects: data frames, tibbles and tsibbles.
- When the object has several columns, the series is the column named by `var`, or the only numeric column if there is exactly one (e.g. a tibble with a date column and a value column). Otherwise `var` is required.
- A tsibble must hold a single series (at most one key value), be regular, and have no implicit gaps; gaps must be filled explicitly by the user.
- A plain data frame carries no frequency, so equal spacing cannot be checked; if it has exactly one date-time column, that column must be strictly increasing.
- Missing or non-finite values are an **error**. Nothing is dropped silently.
- Irregularly spaced `zoo`/`xts` series are an error.
- Backends that drop missing values internally (e.g. `urca::ur.ers`, which applies `na.omit`) are only called after these checks.

## Deterministic specifications

| Code | Meaning | Accepted aliases |
|---|---|---|
| `"n"` | no constant, no trend | `"none"` |
| `"c"` | constant | `"drift"` (urca), `"constant"`, `"intercept"` (bootUR) |
| `"ct"` | constant and linear trend | `"trend"` |

Aliases are mapped to the canonical code on input; results always report the canonical code. `"ctt"` (quadratic trend) is reserved and not part of v0.1.

The time index is $t = 1,\dots,T$ in the original sample, so the trend coefficient has the same meaning in every regression of a procedure regardless of the effective sample.

# The ADF regression

## Regressions

$$
\Delta y_t = a + \gamma t + b\,y_{t-1} + \sum_{j=1}^{k}\beta_j \Delta y_{t-j} + \varepsilon_t,
$$

with $a=\gamma=0$ imposed for `"n"` and $\gamma = 0$ for `"c"`. The unit-root null is $H_0: b = 0$ against $H_1: b<0$.

## Statistics

| Statistic | Regression | Null | Reference distribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\tau_1$ | `n` | $b=0$ | Dickey–Fuller, no deterministics |
| $\tau_2$ ($\tau_\mu$) | `c` | $b=0$ | Dickey–Fuller, constant |
| $\tau_3$ ($\tau_\tau$) | `ct` | $b=0$ | Dickey–Fuller, constant and trend |
| $\phi_1$ | `c` | $a=b=0$ | Dickey–Fuller (1981) |
| $\phi_2$ | `ct` | $a=\gamma=b=0$ | Dickey–Fuller (1981) |
| $\phi_3$ | `ct` | $\gamma=b=0$ | Dickey–Fuller (1981) |

The $\phi$ statistics are computed from nested regressions **on the same effective sample**:

$$
\phi = \frac{(RSS_R - RSS_U)/r}{RSS_U/(N - p_U)},
$$

where $r$ is the number of restrictions, $N$ the effective sample size and $p_U$ the number of parameters in the unrestricted regression.

$\phi_2$ is computed and reported but is not used by any strategy in @sec-strategies; it is included because users (and urca) expect it.

## Effective sample

With $k$ lagged differences, observations $t = k+2,\dots,T$ are usable, so $N = T-k-1$.

When lags are selected from $0,\dots,k_{\max}$, all candidates are estimated on the **common sample** $t = k_{\max}+2,\dots,T$, with $N = T - k_{\max} - 1$.

::: {.callout-important}
**Decision D1 (settled): sample of the final regression after lag selection.**

- (a) *Common sample*: the final regression keeps $t = k_{\max}+2,\dots,T$.
- (b) *Maximal sample*: the final regression is re-estimated on $t = k^*+2,\dots,T$ for the selected $k^*$.

Convention: (a) by default, with (b) available as `final_sample = "maximal"` (useful in small samples, where (a) discards $k_{\max}-k^*$ observations). Inside a specification strategy, all regressions use one common sample (required for the $\phi$ statistics and for comparable decisions). Each implementation conforms; any existing divergence is recorded.
:::

## Minimum sample

- The fit is refused if $N \le p_U + 1$, i.e. at least two residual degrees of freedom are required (this applies to every regression the package fits).
- A warning is issued when $N < 25$, the smallest sample size in the tabulated critical values.
- Specification strategies require $N \ge 25$ (as in Python).

# Lag selection

## Criteria

Candidates are $k = 0,\dots,k_{\max}$, all on the common sample of size $N = T-k_{\max}-1$. With $\hat\sigma^2_k = N^{-1}\sum \hat e_{t,k}^2$:

| Criterion | Definition |
|---|---|
| AIC | $\ln\hat\sigma^2_k + 2k/N$ |
| BIC | $\ln\hat\sigma^2_k + k\ln N / N$ |
| MAIC | $\ln\hat\sigma^2_k + 2\{\tau_N(k)+k\}/N$ |
| MBIC | $\ln\hat\sigma^2_k + \ln N\,\{\tau_N(k)+k\}/N$ |

where (Ng and Perron 2001)

$$
\tau_N(k) = \hat\sigma_k^{-2}\,\hat\beta_0^2 \sum_{t} \tilde y_{t-1}^2 ,
$$

with $\tilde y_t$ the detrended series and $\hat\beta_0$ the coefficient on $\tilde y_{t-1}$ in the regression of $\Delta\tilde y_t$ on $\tilde y_{t-1}$ and $k$ lagged differences of $\tilde y_t$.

Deterministic parameters are common to all candidates and do not enter the penalty.

AIC and BIC are computed from the ADF regression itself (with its deterministic terms). MAIC and MBIC are computed, as in Ng and Perron (2001), from the regression of $\Delta\tilde y_t$ on $\tilde y_{t-1}$ and $k$ lagged differences of the detrended series, with no deterministic terms; both $\hat\sigma^2_k$ and $\tau_N(k)$ come from that regression. The detrending is OLS on the deterministic terms over the full sample $t = 1,\dots,T$ (none for `"n"`).

When the user fixes the lag order, no selection takes place and the regression uses the maximal sample $t = k+2,\dots,T$ (as urca does).

::: {.callout-important}
**Decision D2 (settled): detrending used inside MAIC/MBIC.**
Convention: OLS detrending under the test's deterministic specification for ADF. For GLS-based tests (Phase 2), Perron and Qu (2007) is to be followed. Each implementation conforms; any existing divergence is recorded.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
**Decision D3 (settled): default $k_{\max}$.**
Convention: $k_{\max} = \lfloor 12\,(T/100)^{1/4} \rfloor$ (Schwert 1989), as used with MAIC by Ng and Perron (2001); always reported in the result. Each implementation conforms; any existing divergence is recorded.
:::

## Reporting

`select_lags()` returns the full criterion table (every $k$ and every criterion), the selected $k^*$, $k_{\max}$, the common sample and the detrending used, not only the selected order. Ties are broken in favour of the smaller $k$.

# Critical values and calibration

Each result records its **calibration**: the method, the source and any approximation.

| Method | Use in v0.1 |
|---|---|
| `table` | Tabulated finite-sample critical values |
| `response_surface` | Critical values or p-values from a response-surface regression |
| `conventional_t` | Student-$t$ reference distribution (conditional tests in strategies) |
| `bootstrap` | Phase 2 onwards (bootUR adapter), Phase 3 (own engine) |

::: {.callout-important}
**Decision D4 (settled): source of $\tau$ critical values.**
Convention: MacKinnon (2010) finite-sample response surfaces at the 1%, 5% and 10% levels, evaluated at the effective $N$. For `"n"`, which MacKinnon (2010) did not update, the MacKinnon (1996) surface is used; the result records which. P-values (MacKinnon 1994/1996) are reported only when the implementation computes them. Each implementation conforms, since decisions near the boundary depend on the source.
:::

**$\phi$ critical values (v0.1):** Dickey–Fuller (1981), as reproduced in Enders' Table B. Lookup rule (as in Python): use the largest tabulated sample size not exceeding $N$, capped at 500. This is a documented approximation, recorded as such in the result (with the table row used), and is scheduled for replacement by response surfaces in Phase 2. For $N < 25$ the $T = 25$ row is used and flagged as an extrapolation.

Two differences from urca 1.3-4 are deliberate: (i) urca uses the next *larger* tabulated sample size (e.g. the $T = 50$ row for $25 \le N < 50$), which is less conservative; (ii) urca's $\phi_3$ row for $T = 250$ repeats the $T = 100$ values at 5% and 10% (6.49, 5.47); the published values are 6.34 and 5.39.

# The result contract {#sec-contract}

Every test returns an object of class `ur_test` (R) / `URTestResult` (Python) with the following fields, whatever engine computed it.

| Field | Type | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `method` | string | Full name of the test, e.g. `"Augmented Dickey-Fuller test"` |
| `test` | string | Test family, e.g. `"ADF"`, `"KPSS"` |
| `statistic_name` | string | e.g. `"tau3"`, `"phi3"`, `"Z_tau"` |
| `statistic` | number | Value of the statistic |
| `null`, `alternative` | string | Hypotheses in words, e.g. `"unit root"` / `"stationary around a linear trend"` |
| `trend` | string | Canonical deterministic code |
| `lags` | integer | Lagged differences (ADF-type) or bandwidth (PP/KPSS); `bandwidth_rule` stated separately |
| `lag_selection` | record or null | Method, $k_{\max}$, criterion table, detrending (null when lags were fixed by the user) |
| `nobs` | integer | Effective sample size $N$ |
| `sample` | pair of integers | First and last $t$ of the effective sample |
| `critical_values` | named numbers | At least levels 0.01, 0.05, 0.10 |
| `tail` | string | `"lower"` (rejects for small values: unit-root tests) or `"upper"` (rejects for large values: KPSS, $\phi$); critical values must be ordered consistently |
| `p_value` | number or missing | Only when the calibration provides one; never interpolated from three critical values |
| `calibration` | record | Method, source, approximation note (e.g. "table lookup at N=100") |
| `level`, `reject` | number, logical | Decision at the chosen level (default 0.05): from the critical value at that level when available, otherwise from the p-value; an error if neither exists |
| `other_statistics` | named numbers | e.g. the $\phi$ statistics accompanying $\tau_3$ |
| `other_critical_values` | named list | Optional: critical values for entries of `other_statistics` (same format as `critical_values`, upper tail), each with its source |
| `engine` | string | e.g. `"internal 0.1.0"`, `"urca 1.3-4"` |
| `warnings` | strings | Small-sample and approximation warnings |
| `regression` | record or null | Fitted regression (coefficients, standard errors, RSS, residuals); may be omitted for speed |
| `call` | language | The call (R only) |

Methods (R): `print` and `summary`; `tidy` and `glance` (via `generics`) are planned, not yet implemented. `print` states the null hypothesis, statistic, critical values and their source, and the decision in words; `summary` adds the calibration details, accompanying statistics, lag-selection table and test regression.

`validate_ur_test()` checks every field of this contract, including that the stored decision agrees with the statistic, critical values, tail, p-value and level. The constructor never truncates: a non-whole `lags`, `nobs` or `sample` is an error.

# Specification strategies {#sec-strategies}

## Common structure

R interface: `ur_strategy(y, strategy = c("original", "conservative", "hamilton"), trending, allow_no_constant, lags, max_lags, criterion, level)`. Every test in a sequence uses the same `level`, which must be one of the tabulated levels (0.01, 0.05, 0.10).

The decision logic is a pure function of the individual rejection decisions (no data). All statistics a strategy may need are computed first, on one common sample with one lag order, and the path is then read off. This makes every branch testable with constructed decisions and the whole procedure bootstrappable (Phase 4).

The tests in a history are labelled `tau3`, `phi3`, `aux_trend` (t test of the trend with $b = 0$ imposed), `cond_ct` (conditional t test of $b$ with the trend retained), `tau2`, `phi1`, `aux_const`, `cond_c` and `tau1`. The terminal test is returned as a `ur_test`: an ADF result for the $\tau$ tests, or a conditional $t$ test (calibration `conventional_t`, Student $t$ with the residual degrees of freedom, with a p-value) for `cond_ct` and `cond_c`.

A strategy returns an object of class `ur_strategy` with:

- `strategy`, `settings` (including permissions such as `allow_no_constant`);
- `specification`: the chosen deterministic code;
- `terminal`: the `ur_test` of the terminal test;
- `unit_root_rejected`: logical, the final decision;
- `lags`, `nobs`, `sample`: shared by every regression in the sequence;
- `history`: one row per step (below);
- `engine`, `call`.

Lag order: selected **once** under `"ct"` (method and $k_{\max}$ as supplied) and held fixed throughout the sequence, as in Python. For Hamilton's rule, lags are selected under the declared specification.

**History columns:** `step`, `stage` (`T`, `C`, `N`), `regression` (`ct`, `c`, `n`, `aux_ct`, `aux_c`), `test`, `null` (in words), `statistic`, `critical_value`, `level`, `calibration`, `reject`, `rejection_type`, `next_action`, `reason`.

`rejection_type` distinguishes three cases that must never be confused:

1. `unit_root`: rejection of the unit-root null by a $\tau$ or terminal conditional test;
2. `joint_restriction`: rejection by $\phi_1$ or $\phi_3$ (a decision about the path, not about the unit root);
3. `deterministic`: rejection of a deterministic-coefficient restriction in an auxiliary regression (also a path decision).

No p-value is reported for the sequence as a whole. Overall size is a property to be established by simulation or by bootstrapping the whole procedure (Phases 3–4).

## Original (Dolado–Jenkinson–Sosvilla-Rivero / Enders)

::: {.callout-note}
**Verified** (2 November 2026) against Enders, *Supplementary Manual*, 4th ed., Section 4.4 (Steps 1–4 and Figure A2.1), which follows Dolado, Jenkinson and Sosvilla-Rivero (1990).

- *Notation.* Enders writes $\gamma$ for the coefficient on $y_{t-1}$ and $a_2$ for the trend coefficient; this specification writes $b$ and $\gamma$ respectively.
- *Conventions not fixed by the source.* The manual says to test the lagged-level coefficient "using a t-distribution" without stating the tail, and to test the deterministic coefficients with a "standard t-test". The tails and reference distribution are therefore this specification's convention (Decision D5), not Enders'.
- *Figure A2.1.* At the constant-only stage the figure says "Go to Step 2" where the text returns to the constant-only regression; the text governs.
- *Interpretation of the terminal branches.* When the trend is retained and $b = 0$ is not rejected, Enders concludes that the series has a unit root and a quadratic trend; when the constant is retained and $b = 0$ is not rejected, a unit root with drift.
:::

**Stage T** (regression `ct`):

1. Test $b=0$ with $\tau_3$. Rejection: stop; no unit root, specification `ct`.
2. Otherwise test $\gamma=b=0$ with $\phi_3$. Non-rejection: go to Stage C.
3. If $\phi_3$ rejects: in the auxiliary regression imposing $b=0$, test $\gamma=0$ (two-sided $t$).
   - Not significant: go to Stage C.
   - Significant: the trend is retained. Test $b=0$ in the `ct` regression with the conditional conventional $t$ test (lower tail). Terminal.

**Stage C** (regression `c`):

4. Test $b=0$ with $\tau_2$. Rejection: stop; no unit root, specification `c`.
5. Otherwise test $a=b=0$ with $\phi_1$. Non-rejection: go to Stage N.
6. If $\phi_1$ rejects: in the auxiliary regression imposing $b=0$, test $a=0$ (two-sided $t$).
   - Not significant: go to Stage N.
   - Significant: test $b=0$ in the `c` regression with the conditional conventional $t$ test (lower tail). Terminal.

**Stage N** (regression `n`):

7. Test $b=0$ with $\tau_1$. Terminal.

::: {.callout-important}
**Decision D5 (settled): conditional tests.** Convention: Student-$t$ reference with the residual degrees of freedom of the regression concerned (asymptotically equivalent to $N(0,1)$, slightly more conservative in small samples); lower tail for $b$, two-sided for $a$ and $\gamma$.
:::

## Conservative

Identical to the original at Stage T and at step 4. If $\tau_2$ does not reject, the constant is **retained** and the procedure stops: the terminal decision is the non-rejection by $\tau_2$. No conditional conventional $t$ test is used to justify retention.

With `allow_no_constant = TRUE`, the original steps 5–7 are evaluated. This is permission to consider the restricted model, not an instruction to select it.

The conservative strategy is an experimental proposal; its documentation must say that its overall size has not been established.

## Hamilton (rule-based)

Hamilton (1994, ch. 17) chooses the regression so that both hypotheses are plausible descriptions of the series. The choice is made **by the user, before testing**:

- `trending = TRUE`: regression `ct`, terminal test $\tau_3$ (Hamilton's Case 4);
- `trending = FALSE`: regression `c`, terminal test $\tau_2$ (Case 2).

Rules:

- `trending` has **no default** and no data-driven fallback. A data-driven choice would turn the rule into another pre-test procedure.
- The result records that the specification came from a user declaration (`reason = "declared by user"`).
- A descriptive helper (plot and sample mean of $\Delta y_t$) may be offered; its output is labelled descriptive, not inferential.

**Case 3 (optional, experimental):** regression `c` with a non-zero drift under the null, where the $t$ statistic on $b$ is asymptotically $N(0,1)$ (West 1988). Available only as `inference = "west_normal"`. The result reports the estimated drift relative to its standard error and warns when that ratio is small, since the normal approximation is then poor.

::: {.callout-important}
**Decision D6 (settled):** Case 3 is deferred to the specification-uncertainty phase (v0.4), where it is introduced together with the Monte Carlo harness (which can show how the normal approximation degrades as the drift shrinks). The warning threshold is set then.
:::

# Validation standard {#sec-validation}

Three levels:

1. **Bitwise reproducibility:** desirable, not required.
2. **Numerical reproducibility:** required, with justified tolerances. Default: $|x - x_{\text{ref}}| \le 10^{-10}|x_{\text{ref}}| + 10^{-12}$ for statistics, coefficients and critical values computed by formula; looser tolerances must be justified in the fixture.
3. **Statistical reproducibility:** required for Monte Carlo results. Rejection frequencies agree within Monte Carlo error (two-proportion test).

Decision agreement is checked separately. Any disagreement is logged with $|\text{statistic} - \text{critical value}|$; disagreements are acceptable only within numerical tolerance of the boundary.

**Published fixture for the strategies.** Enders' U.S. real-GDP example (log real GDP, 1947Q1–2012Q4, one lagged difference) is stored in `inst/fixtures/enders_rgdp.csv` with its provenance and expected values in `enders_rgdp.json`. The regressions have $N = 262$ observations (Enders' text mentions 244, but the regression output and the data imply 262). The example reports $\tau_3 = -1.49$, $\phi_3 = 2.97$, $\tau_2 = -2.05$, $\phi_1 = 25.49$ and $t(a_0) = 6.80$ in the auxiliary regression; the original procedure then rejects through the conditional $t$ test, while the conservative procedure retains the constant and does not reject. With $N = 262$, both Enders and this specification use the $T = 250$ table row for $\phi$. Published values are rounded, so they are checked to half a unit in the last printed digit; the intercept $t$ value in (A2.3), printed as 2.64, equals 2.646 (truncation in the source).

References are independent of the implementation under test: independent QR or high-precision (`mpmath`) calculations, published examples, and backend packages.

**Shared fixtures** live in `inst/fixtures/` (R) and the equivalent Python directory, as JSON files with: `id`, `description`, `source` (with provenance and data hash), `data`, `settings`, `expected`, `tolerance`.

# Known backend limitations (urca 1.3-4)

Checked against the urca 1.3-4 reference documentation. Each limitation is the documented reason for replacing an adapter with an internal implementation.

| Function | Limitation | Consequence for `unitroottools` |
|---|---|---|
| `ur.df` | Lag selection only `"Fixed"`, `"AIC"`, `"BIC"`; no MAIC/MBIC; sample convention for comparing lags not documented | ADF is internal from v0.1 |
| `ur.df` | Object reports tabulated critical values, no p-value (urca does export MacKinnon p-value functions separately) | Calibration handled in our own layer |
| `ur.df` | No auxiliary regressions, conditional tests or decision sequence | Strategies are internal |
| `ur.pp` | Bartlett kernel only; bandwidth `"short"`/`"long"` or user-specified; `model` only `"constant"`/`"trend"` | Adapter exposes exactly these options; internal version in Phase 2 |
| `ur.kpss` | Bandwidth `"short"`/`"long"`/`"nil"` or user-specified; no automatic (Newey–West, Andrews) bandwidth | As above |
| `ur.ers` | DF-GLS: `lag.max` is the fixed number of lagged differences, no lag selection; P-test selects lags by BIC; applies `na.omit` internally | Adapter validates input first; MAIC version in Phase 2 |
| — | No Ng–Perron M-tests | Internal implementation in Phase 2 |
| all | S4 objects, no common result, no decision or provenance | `ur_test` contract over every backend |

# Decisions

| ID | Topic | Convention | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | Final-regression sample after lag selection | Common sample by default; maximal as option | Settled |
| D2 | Detrending inside MAIC/MBIC | OLS detrending | Settled |
| D3 | Default $k_{\max}$ | Schwert $\lfloor 12(T/100)^{1/4}\rfloor$ | Settled |
| D4 | $\tau$ critical values | MacKinnon (2010) response surfaces | Settled |
| D5 | Conditional tests in strategies | Student-$t$, lower tail for $b$ | Settled |
| D6 | Hamilton Case 3 | Deferred to v0.4 (with the Monte Carlo harness) | Settled |

- Hamilton, J. D. (1994). *Time Series Analysis*. Princeton University Press, ch. 17.
- MacKinnon, J. G. (1996). Numerical distribution functions for unit root and cointegration tests. *Journal of Applied Econometrics*, 11, 601–618.
- MacKinnon, J. G. (2010). Critical values for cointegration tests. Queen's Economics Department Working Paper 1227.
- Ng, S. and Perron, P. (2001). Lag length selection and the construction of unit root tests with good size and power. *Econometrica*, 69, 1519–1554.
- Perron, P. and Qu, Z. (2007). A simple modification to improve the finite sample properties of Ng and Perron's unit root tests. *Economics Letters*, 94, 12–19.
- Pfaff, B. urca: Unit Root and Cointegration Tests for Time Series Data, R package version 1.3-4.
- Schwert, G. W. (1989). Tests for unit roots: a Monte Carlo investigation. *Journal of Business & Economic Statistics*, 7, 147–159.
